pages.title: Yunus Emre and Sufism
pages.content:
Yunus Emre was a great Anatolian poet and Muslim mystic (Sufi). A Sufi is a person who seeks closeness to Allah by adopting Islamic mysticism. Sufis maintain a lifestyle within the outer (visible) and inner norms of Islam. The outer part relates to the body’s acts of worship, whereas the inner side handles the morality and intentions of the heart. Sufis adhere to moral principles that include the pursuit of becoming better people, the ability to remain patient during difficult times, the act of giving generously without expecting any return, the act of doing good to all individuals without prejudice, the response to evil with kindness, and not attaching importance to worldly possessions such as wealth, status, and fame.

In addition to his standing as a Sufi, Yunus Emre was one of the first to create and perform poetry from the heart in plain Turkish. He was also one of the Turkish poets to play a crucial role in the development of Old Anatolian Turkish. The words and expressions that he used made a significant contribution to the development of Turkish as a literary language. He established a literary tradition based on Sufism. One of the most important factors in the popularity of Yunus Emre’s works among the public is his style.

It shows that the outer part is the cause of the inner side.
It contrasts two different sides of the same lifestyle, and Sufis keep both.

pages.title: His Style and Education
pages.content:
His style is neither too simple nor too complex. Thus, his works both have literary value and are easy to understand. His philosophy includes fundamental values that have a significant influence on Turkish culture and ethics in Turkish society.

According to historical accounts, he was a contemporary of famous figures such as Haji Bektash Veli, Mevlana Jalal al-Din Rumi, and Saru Saltuk. According to the widely accepted view, he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21. He is considered the founder of Turkish Sufi literature.

Some sources note that he received a good madrasa education and had a strong knowledge of Arabic, Persian, and the Islamic sciences of his time. However, his education was not limited to madrasas. He also studied both divine love and morals at the tekke, which was a place where Sufi education was taught under the guidance of a sheikh (spiritual tutor).

At that time, tekkes were not just institutions that offered Sufi training but they were also important civil society organizations that strengthened social solidarity and cooperation and also received support from government officials of their time.

languageFocusExercises.title: Keep the Source Caution
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the version that is just as sure as the writer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “According to the widely accepted view, he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21.” Which version is just as sure?
options: It has been proven beyond doubt that he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21.
Most scholars accept that he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21.
Nobody has any idea when he was born or when he died.
Only one old source claims that he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “The widely accepted view” means that many, but not necessarily all, experts agree. “Most scholars accept that …” keeps this broad but not absolute agreement. “Proven beyond doubt” overclaims, “Nobody has any idea” ignores the agreement, and “Only one old source” underclaims it.

feedback.correct: Correct. The rewrite keeps broad agreement without turning it into certainty.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at the second paragraph of Chapter 2. Does “widely accepted” mean proven, unknown, or accepted by many?

languageFocusExercises.title: Balanced Style, Wider Education
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 2 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words complete the lines about his style and his education?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: His style is [blank] too simple [blank] too complex. Thus, his works [blank] have literary value and are easy to understand. … However, his education was not [blank] to madrasas.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Neither … nor …” rejects both extremes and places the style in the middle. “Both … and …” gives the works two qualities at once. “Not limited to” widens the scope: His education included the madrasa but went beyond it, to the tekke. “Either … or” would offer a choice, which the text does not.

feedback.correct: Correct. The style avoids two extremes, the works have two qualities, and his education reaches beyond the madrasa.
feedback.incorrect: Check the first and third paragraphs of Chapter 2. Remember that “neither” pairs with “nor”, and “both” pairs with “and”.

pages.title: Tekkes and Difficult Times
pages.content:
Besides, tekkes were leading institutions in the field of the fine arts, particularly poetry. Many of the great masters of Turkish poetry were trained in tekkes. Yunus Emre was also one of the great masters of poetry who had been trained under his sheikh, Taptuk Emre.

The 13th and 14th centuries, the period in which Yunus Emre was born and lived, coincided with hard times. In those years, the Anatolian Seljuks were severely weakened by the Babai uprisings. This was immediately followed by the defeat at Kösedağ. The defeat at Kösedağ facilitated the Mongols' invasion of Anatolia. Anatolia faced political, economic, and social hardships as a result of these assaults. Society was struggling to cope with these trials.

If we take a closer look at this historical atmosphere, we can better understand Anatolia—the land where Yunus Emre lived and recited his unforgettable verses.

The rule of the Anatolian Seljuk Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I (1220–1237) was the most powerful and glorious period of the Seljuks. He expanded the country’s borders and established a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Coincided with” and “was followed by” place events in time. “Facilitated” (made easier) and “as a result of” link causes and results. “If we take a closer look …, we can better understand …” is a condition that turns history into a tool for interpreting Yunus.

feedback.correct: Correct. The chapter builds a chain from time to cause and then to interpretation.

pages.title: The Babai Uprisings
pages.content:
At the time of his death, the Seljuks were the most powerful and largest state in the Middle East. However, due to the poor governance of his son, Kaykhusraw II (1237–1246), the Seljuk economic and social structure began to decline. Starting in the 13th century, the Turkmen population grew in Anatolia. When the migrations caused by the Mongol invasion were added to this, the lives of people in Anatolia were totally turned upside down. The nomadic Oguz and Turkmen tribes, who had migrated to Anatolia from Central Asia to escape the Mongol invasion, were exhausted from wandering and were looking for safe lands to settle in. This crowd of nomads was also causing unrest within the community. Kaykhusraw II’s failure to manage this situation even worsened the social and economic chaos.

Throughout history, societies that faced difficult circumstances have always awaited a divine figure to save them. The Turkmen, too, were awaiting such a figure. In 1240, they rebelled under the leadership of Baba Ishak, who was a follower of Baba Ilyas. Baba Ilyas was the founder of a non-Sunni religious–mystical movement.

exercises.title: Waiting for a Savior

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Even” Add?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 4. Then choose what “even” adds.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Kaykhusraw II’s failure to manage this situation even worsened the social and economic chaos.” What does “even” show?
options: The chaos began only because of his failure.
The chaos already existed, and his failure made it still worse.
His failure made the chaos less serious than before.
His failure and the chaos happened at different times.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Even” before “worsened” shows intensification: The chaos already existed because of poor governance, population growth and migration, and the sultan’s failure added to it. The chapter does not give a single cause.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Even” shows that an already serious situation became worse.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the causes listed before this sentence in Chapter 4. Was the chaos already there before his failure?

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.

errorItems.sentence: However, because the poor governance of his son, Kaykhusraw II (1237–1246), the Seljuk economic and social structure began to decline.
The nomadic Oguz and Turkmen tribes, who had migrated to Anatolia from Central Asia for escape the Mongol invasion, were exhausted from wandering …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Due to” (like “because of”) is followed by a noun phrase: “due to the poor governance of his son”. “Because” and “since” need a full clause with a verb. Purpose is expressed with “to + verb”: “to escape the Mongol invasion”.

feedback.correct: Correct. A noun phrase follows “due to”, and “to + verb” shows purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Check the first paragraph of Chapter 4: what comes after “due to”, and how does the text say why the tribes migrated?

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.

The passive “were turned upside down” focuses on the people affected; the active “they turned … upside down” puts the migrations first as the cause.

pages.title: Kösedağ and the Mongols
pages.content:
In the eyes of the Turkmen, these spiritual fathers were divine saviors. The rebellion spread rapidly; the Turkmen achieved significant success. In the end, the Seljuk forces suppressed the rebellion with great difficulty and put the rebels to the sword.

However, this situation gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack the Seljuk Empire. In late 1242, the Mongols captured Erzurum and killed its people with swords. This disaster caused deep sorrow and fear among the Seljuk people.

Finally, in 1243, the Seljuk army and the Mongols clashed at Kösedağ, 80 km northeast of Sivas. The Mongols, using the classic false retreat and circling tactic, wiped out the Seljuk forces. Following their easy victory at Kösedağ, the Mongols destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri, and Erzincan, leaving not a single stone standing. They slaughtered the men with swords; women and children were taken captive and forced to follow the Mongol army. Throughout Yunus’s life, this Mongol storm swept across Anatolia like a roller, leaving behind blood, misery, and ruins. Sources say: “The Mongols slaughtered the people of the great cities and towns so mercilessly that hardly anyone remained there.”

exercises.title: Why Now?
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use Chapter 5.
exercises.question: According to the chapter, what gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack the Seljuks?
options: The Seljuk forces had only put down the Turkmen rebellion with great difficulty.
The Seljuk army had just been defeated at Kösedağ.
The Seljuks had already made an agreement with the Mongols.
exercises.explanation: The first paragraph ends with the Seljuks suppressing the rebellion “with great difficulty”. The next paragraph begins: “However, this situation gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack.” Kösedağ came later, in 1243, and the agreement is described in Chapter 6.

feedback.correct: Yes. “This situation” points back to the hard struggle against the rebellion, which showed that the Seljuks were weak.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the start of the second paragraph: “However, this situation …”. Then read the end of the first paragraph to find what “this situation” means.

languageFocusExercises.title: Following the Connectors
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the sentences from Chapter 5 in order. The first words can help.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened between the rebellion and the destruction of the cities?

sequencingItems.text: In the end, the Seljuk forces suppressed the rebellion with great difficulty …
However, this situation gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack the Seljuk Empire.
In late 1242, the Mongols captured Erzurum and killed its people with swords.
Finally, in 1243, the Seljuk army and the Mongols clashed at Kösedağ, 80 km northeast of Sivas.
Following their easy victory at Kösedağ, the Mongols destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri, and Erzincan …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “In the end” closes the rebellion. “However” turns to an unexpected result: The Seljuk victory made them look weak, and this encouraged the Mongols. A date (“In late 1242”) moves the story on, “Finally” marks the decisive battle at the end of a long process, and “Following their easy victory” links the battle to what happened after it.

feedback.correct: Correct. The connectors lead from the rebellion, through a turning point, to the battle and its aftermath.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each connector needs before it: “However” needs a situation to turn from, “Finally” comes near the end, and “Following their victory” needs the battle first. Then check Chapter 5.

languageFocusExercises.title: The Language of Destruction
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 5 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the writer show how terrible the destruction was?

matchingPairs.right: defeated the army so completely that it no longer existed

matchingPairs.left: leaving not a single stone standing
matchingPairs.right: so that no building remained

matchingPairs.left: swept across Anatolia like a roller
matchingPairs.right: moved over the land, crushing everything in its path
almost nobody was left alive

correctAnswer.wiped out the Seljuk forces: defeated the army so completely that it no longer existed
correctAnswer.swept across Anatolia like a roller: moved over the land, crushing everything in its path

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter uses strong verbs (“wiped out”), a simile (“like a roller”) and extreme negatives (“not a single stone”, “hardly anyone”) to show the scale of the disaster. Notice that the most extreme description is introduced with “Sources say:”. The writer attributes it to historical sources rather than presenting it as his own measurement.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each expression intensifies the picture of destruction.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 5 again and look at what each expression describes: an army, buildings, a whole region or the people of the cities.

Following this easy victory, they destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri and Erzincan. As a result, ordinary people suffered: Men were killed, and women and children were taken captive. Sources say that hardly anyone remained in the great cities and towns. For this reason, the battle became the start of a long Mongol storm across Anatolia.

pages.title: Anatolia Under Pressure
pages.content:
The weakening of the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya led to the rapid emergence of small principalities in Anatolia. They were also in constant conflict over the throne, wealth, and summer and winter pastures. The Ottoman state was still a small principality at that time.

These events created an atmosphere of panic in Anatolia that had never been seen before. In the end, an agreement was reached with the Mongols, but in time the Seljuks became a dependent state of the Mongols. The Seljuk sultans began to act almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials. A significant part of state income began to be sent to the Mongols every year. However, this tax increased constantly and this made both the state and the people poorer.

Statesmen like Jalal al-Din Karatay, while on the one hand trying to manage the Mongols, were also making efforts to provide some relief to the state and the people. Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough. Finally, in 1308, the lands of Anatolia were directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire (the Mongol state centred in Iran).

exercises.title: Were the Efforts Enough?
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 6.
exercises.question: According to the chapter, statesmen like Jalal al-Din Karatay managed to stop Anatolia from coming under direct Mongol rule.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says these statesmen tried to manage the Mongols and bring “some relief to the state and the people”. “Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough. Finally, in 1308, the lands of Anatolia were directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The writer values their efforts but says clearly that they “were not enough”; in 1308 Anatolia was directly attached to the Ilkhanate.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph again. Look at the word “Nevertheless” and at what happened in 1308.

languageFocusExercises.title: Almost Like Officials
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 6. Then choose what it means.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The Seljuk sultans began to act almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials.” What does the writer mean?
options: The sultans officially became Mongol civil servants and gave up their titles.
The sultans still had their titles, but they had so little freedom that they behaved like officials serving the Mongols.
The sultans made the Mongols work as civil officials in the Seljuk state.
The sultans pretended to obey the Mongols but secretly kept full control.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As if” introduces a comparison with something that is not literally true, and the past form “were” marks it as unreal. “Almost” weakens it further. The sultans were still sultans, but their behavior resembled that of subordinate officials, which shows how dependent the state had become.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Almost as if” compares their behavior to that of officials without saying they really became officials.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the sentence before it: The Seljuks “became a dependent state of the Mongols”. Does “as if” state a fact or make a comparison?

languageFocusExercises.title: Stages of Dependency
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 6 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words show the steps, and that the efforts were not enough?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: In the end, an agreement was reached with the Mongols, but [blank] the Seljuks became a dependent state of the Mongols. … Statesmen like Jalal al-Din Karatay, [blank] on the one hand trying to manage the Mongols, were also making efforts to provide some relief to the state and the people. [blank], these efforts were not enough. [blank], in 1308, the lands of Anatolia were directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire …
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “In time” shows a slow change after the agreement. “While” (+ -ing) shows two things the statesmen did at the same moment; “during” would need a noun. “Nevertheless” accepts the effort but says it failed; “Therefore” would wrongly make the failure a result of the effort. “Finally” marks the last stage of the process, not the beginning.

feedback.correct: Correct. The words show a gradual process, parallel efforts, their limit and the final stage.
feedback.incorrect: Check the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 6. Which blank needs a contrast with a positive effort, and which one marks the last stage?

languageFocusExercises.title: Same Result, New Words
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.

In a clause, the same events become verbs: the sultanate weakened, principalities emerged. In the second item, “this made them poorer” becomes a result clause after “Because …”.

feedback.incorrect: Turn the noun into a verb in the past simple (emergence → emerged) or ask what happened to the state and the people. Then check the first and second paragraphs of Chapter 6.

pages.title: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
pages.content:
Anatolia was experiencing total chaos. During the same period, the shaykhs from the regions of Turkestan, Transoxiana, Khorasan, Khwarezm and Iran came to Anatolia under Mongol pressure. These shaykhs raised dervishes on their teachings; these dervishes were dominant among nomads. They were spreading a simple understanding of Islam and establishing a kind of popular Sufism.

So in such an environment, Yunus Emre emerged as a wise dervish and traveled around Anatolia. He tried to respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life in hard days through the lens of his Sufi identity, using poetry as his medium.

Yunus’s understanding of Sufism is based on the Qur’an and the Sunnah, which is the collective term for the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet (pbuh), as well as on the thoughts and experiences of the Muslim Sufis who lived before him. In his poems, he expresses a vivid love for Allah as a way of life, along with fear of Allah and faithfulness to the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

exercises.title: A Poet in Hard Days
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use Chapter 7.
exercises.question: How does the writer describe Yunus Emre’s response to the chaos in Anatolia?
options: He tried to help people make sense of life, using poetry and his Sufi point of view.
He brought the chaos in Anatolia to an end with his poems.
He came to Anatolia from Khorasan under Mongol pressure, like the other shaykhs.
exercises.explanation: The second paragraph says: “He tried to respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life in hard days through the lens of his Sufi identity, using poetry as his medium.” The writer says “tried”; the chapter does not claim that his poems ended the chaos. The shaykhs from Khorasan and other regions are a different group.

feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph again. Look for the verb that describes what Yunus did, and check whether the writer says he succeeded.

languageFocusExercises.title: Circumstance, Perspective and Means
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 7 with its meaning in the chapter.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases tell us about the times and about Yunus?

at the time when this chaos was happening
had the strongest influence on groups who moved from place to place

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Under … pressure” gives the circumstance that caused the shaykhs to move. “During the same period” links two events in time. “Through the lens of” is a metaphor: A lens is something you look through, so it means “from the point of view of”. The participle phrase “using poetry as his medium” adds the means by which he responded.

feedback.correct: Correct. The chapter links a historical circumstance, a point of view and a means of communication.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A participle phrase (“using poetry as his medium”) is a compact way of saying “and he used …”. A relative pronoun (“who”) joins two clauses about the same people without repeating the noun. “Under Mongol pressure” is a short prepositional phrase for a whole cause clause: “because the Mongols pressured them”.

pages.title: Tawhid and True Reality
pages.content:
One of the most important fundamental values in his works is the belief in tawhid, which means the absolute Oneness of Allah. According to Yunus Emre, the Creator, Allah is the source of all things and, therefore, everything is connected to Him. The Creator is the true and only reality. From this perspective, Yunus Emre held the idea of the Unity of Existence. According to the theory of the Unity of Existence, Allah, the absolute reality, desired to be known and to reveal Himself, and for this reason, He created the worlds through His attributes.

Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“The entire universe is Tawhid; Adam (that is, the human being) is the one who knows Tawhid.
Whoever denies this Tawhid is an enemy to his own soul.”
Turkish:
Tevhîd imiş cümle âlem, tevhîdi bilendür Âdem
Bu tevhîdi inkâr iden öz cânına düşmânımış
[/POEM]

As a result of creation, the initial unity disintegrated and multiple existence emerged. Nonetheless, this multiple existence is nothing but manifestations of the names of Allah.

hotspots.title: Unity of Existence
hotspots.description: Yunus held that Allah desired to be known and to reveal Himself, and so created the worlds through His attributes.

hotspots.title: Source of All Things
hotspots.description: For Yunus, Allah is the source of all things and the true and only reality, so everything is connected to Him.

exercises.title: Cause or Result?
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 8.
exercises.question: According to the chapter, Allah created the worlds because the first unity had broken apart into multiple existence.
exercises.explanation: The chapter gives a different reason: Allah “desired to be known and to reveal Himself, and for this reason, He created the worlds through His attributes.” The breaking of unity is a result, not a cause: “As a result of creation, the initial unity disintegrated and multiple existence emerged.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Multiple existence came as a result of creation; the reason for creation was that Allah desired to be known.
feedback.incorrect: Compare two places: “for this reason” at the end of the first paragraph and “As a result of creation” in the last paragraph. Which one came first?

languageFocusExercises.title: Whose View Is It?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the two sentence openings from Chapter 8. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “According to Yunus Emre, the Creator, Allah is the source of all things …” / “According to the theory of the Unity of Existence, Allah, the absolute reality, desired to be known …” Why does the writer begin with “According to …”?
options: To show that the writer disagrees with these ideas.
To show whose view or which theory the ideas belong to.
To show that these are the exact words of a poem.
To show that the ideas were accepted by every scholar.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “According to X” attributes an idea to a person or a school of thought. It does not show disagreement, and it does not claim that everybody accepts the idea. When the chapter quotes Yunus’s actual words, it uses a different frame: “Yunus says:” followed by the verse.

feedback.correct: Correct. “According to” tells the reader whose view is being presented.
feedback.incorrect: Compare “According to …” with “Yunus says:” in Chapter 8. Which one introduces a quotation, and which one reports a view?

languageFocusExercises.title: Linking the Argument

pages.title: Unity and Love
pages.content:
In this sense, everything which is created is a reflection; the only thing that truly exists is Allah. The ultimate purpose of humanity is to reach unity with Allah.

His words remind us of Allah’s commands for achieving this unity.

Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“Anyone who claims to be a Muslim should know the requirements of Islam,
He should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers”
Turkish:
Müslümanım diyen kişi şartı nedir bilse gerek
Tanrı'nın buyruğun tutup beş vakt namaz kılsa gerek
[/POEM]

Love, another important value that stands out in Yunus Emre’s works, lies at the core of his philosophy. He places love at the foundation of the human relationship with the Creator and with His creation. Love for the created is an extension of the love of Allah. Therefore, those who love the Creator love the created, and those who love the created also love the Creator. Love brings unity and harmony.

The purpose of love is to reach Allah and achieve unity in His presence. From this perspective, love and unity, which lie at the essence of his thought, are interrelated. For, according to him, where love is absent, negative emotions such as anger, heartbreak and separation arise.

an image of something else, like one seen in a mirror

pages.title: The Heart and Intellect
pages.content:
Therefore, for Yunus Emre the love and the oneness of Allah are the values at the foundation of moral behavior.

In Yunus Emre’s philosophy, the heart is the center of love. It is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, the place where Allah manifests Himself. For this reason, he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house. Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“The heart is the throne of the Lord, and He looked at the heart.
Whoever destroys the heart is the most unfortunate of the two worlds.”
Turkish:
Gönül Çalab’ın tahtı, Çalap gönüle baktı.
İki cihan bedbahtı, kim gönül yıkar ise.
[/POEM]

In his view, purity of the heart is essential for the proper performance of acts of worship. At the same time, the heart is the eye that perceives the truth and the center of understanding.

Yunus Emre emphasizes not only the heart but also the intellect as a value, describing it as “a light from Allah that has existed since eternity.” According to him, there are three types of intellect: the practical reason, which enables a person to understand how the world works and sustain worldly life; the limited intellect, which teaches a person about the order of the hereafter; and the universal intellect, which guides one to behave with piety.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
deep respect for Allah shown through devoted worship and good conduct
the capacity for reason and understanding, described here as a spiritual and moral faculty
time without beginning or end
a state of being free from moral or spiritual corruption
recognizes, understands, or becomes aware of something

hotspots.title: Throne of the Lord
hotspots.description: In Yunus Emre’s philosophy, the heart is the center of love and is described as “the throne of the Lord.”

hotspots.title: Light from Allah
hotspots.description: Yunus described intellect as “a light from Allah that has existed since eternity” and named three types of it.

exercises.title: Allah’s House
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use Chapter 10.
exercises.question: Why did Yunus describe breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house?
options: He saw the heart as “the throne of the Lord”, the place where Allah manifests Himself.
He called the intellect “a light from Allah that has existed since eternity”.
He believed that, where love is absent, anger and separation arise.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says the heart is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, the place where Allah manifests Himself. “For this reason, he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house.” The other two ideas are in the book, but they are not the reason for this description.

feedback.correct: Yes. “For this reason” links the image of the heart as Allah’s throne to the warning against breaking hearts – a strong call to respect other people.
feedback.incorrect: Find the words “For this reason” in the second paragraph and read the sentence just before them.

languageFocusExercises.title: Three Types of Intellect
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 10 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does Yunus Emre describe intellect and its types?

correctAnswer.“a light from Allah that has existed sin: Yunus’s description of intellect in general

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter defines each type of intellect with a relative clause: “which enables a person to understand how the world works”, “which teaches a person about the order of the hereafter”, “which guides one to behave with piety”. The phrase “describing it as …” introduces how Yunus sees intellect as a whole.

languageFocusExercises.title: Describing and Clarifying
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct word.

errorItems.sentence: Therefore, for Yunus Emre the love and the oneness of Allah is the values at the foundation of moral behavior.
It is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, the place which Allah manifests Himself.
For this reason, he described breaking a heart like destroying Allah’s house.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A subject joined with “and” (“the love and the oneness of Allah”) takes a plural verb: “are the values”. “That is” introduces a clarification, and a place is followed by “where” (or “in which”): “the place where Allah manifests Himself”. The verb “describe” takes “as”: “describe X as Y”. “For this reason” turns the description of the heart into a moral conclusion.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “is described as”, “that is” and “for this reason”. It is an image, not the body.

This is an image about the spiritual heart, not a claim about the body. For this reason, he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house. One moral lesson follows: We should choose our words and actions carefully so that we do not hurt other people’s feelings.

pages.title: Salvation and Death
pages.content:
His understanding of unity is also evident in the relationship between the heart and reason; he emphasizes that for a person to reach salvation, heart and reason must support one another.

Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“May your intelligence / wisdom save you from all troubles
May happiness be yours for all the months and years to come”
Turkish:
Seni dürlü beladan kurtara akl,
Saadet ola sana cümle ay, yıl
[/POEM]

Death is another significant theme in Yunus’s poems. According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity, as the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said: “Those who remember death the most and prepare best for what comes after it are the wisest.” (Ibn Majah, Zuhd, 31, hadith 4259) A person who lives with an understanding of death’s advisory role lives a meaningful and righteous life.

About death Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“Whoever comes into this world must eventually leave it,
A guest in this world, one day they must set out for their homeland”
Turkish:
Bu dünyaya gelen kişi, ahir yine gitse gerek
Misafirdir, vatanına, bir gün sefer etse gerek
[/POEM]

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
a person or influence that gives guidance about how to act or decide
rescue of the soul from sin and punishment, and safety in the life to come
in the end, after some time
having clear importance, purpose, or value
the place a person truly comes from and belongs to; here, the next life

dragDropGroups.group: must: Something is necessary to reach a goal

In the verse about death, “must” expresses inevitability: No one can avoid leaving this world. At the start of a sentence, “May …” expresses a wish or a prayer, not permission or possibility.

feedback.correct: Correct. You saw that “must” can express necessity or inevitability, and that “May …” can express a wish.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “must”, “can” and “rather than”.
discussionPrompts.example: In this chapter, death is presented as the best advisor for humanity rather than as a reason for fear. Yunus reminds us that everyone who comes into this world must leave it one day. Remembering death can help a person to see what really matters. As a result, people can choose a meaningful and righteous life rather than chase things that do not last. This does not happen automatically; it is advice that each person must choose to follow.

pages.title: Morality and Bad Habits
pages.content:
According to Yunus, morality consists of abandoning behaviors unbecoming of humans. In Yunus’s understanding, immoral behaviors are described as “misbehavior” of the animalistic self. Values such as honesty, patience, humility, generosity, respect, trust in Allah, and modesty are important in Yunus Emre’s works. Through these values, Yunus Emre teaches people the path to a righteous life. Additionally, by addressing negative traits such as arrogance, anger, stinginess, greed, envy, backbiting, and slander, he warned people to stay away from these harmful habits. Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide.

Here are some of his verses concerning morality:

Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“I’ve fallen into the prison of greed and cannot escape
It’s a hard, rock-solid place; I cannot break free”
Turkish:
Tamah hapsine düşdüm çıkamazın
Katı berkdür divarı yıkamazın
[/POEM]

In another verse talking about patience, he says:

[POEM]
English:
“Patience is the foundation of a lasting kingdom.
Those blessed with patience will achieve greatness.”
Turkish:
Sabırlu devleti dâim olısar
Nasibi sabr olanlar uluyısar
[/POEM]

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
the quality of not thinking that you are better or more important than others
the lower self associated in the chapter with uncontrolled desires and immoral conduct
a life guided by morally good and correct conduct
harmful qualities of character or behavior
a strong wish to have more money, food or possessions than you need

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the pieces in order to make the sentence about the poems.
languageFocusExercises.question: What two things are Yunus Emre’s poems?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not only … but also …” adds a second, often more surprising, quality to the first. The poems are literary works, and they also guide people’s behavior. The two parts after “not only” and “but also” have the same form (two noun phrases).

feedback.correct: Correct. The sentence gives the poems a literary and a moral function.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the subject and the verb. Then put “not only” before the first quality and “but also” before the second one.

languageFocusExercises.title: Balanced Moral Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph that compares two good values with two bad habits.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which good values and bad habits does the chapter show?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The production task organizes moral contrast without turning it into a vocabulary list.

feedback.correct: Well done. Check that each target pattern carries a clear relationship in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Return to the chapter sentences that use these patterns and model your own sentences on them.

discussionPrompts.question: Use “such as”, “while” and “not only … but also”.
discussionPrompts.example: Yunus Emre’s works praise values such as patience and humility. Patience is called the foundation of a lasting kingdom, while greed is shown as a prison that a person cannot easily escape. Humility brings people closer to others, while arrogance pushes them away. In this way, his poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Which of these is a value in Yunus Emre’s works?
beforeYouRead.quote: Values such as honesty, patience, humility, generosity

iCan: I can name the good values and the bad habits Yunus Emre writes about.
I can say how something is done with “by + -ing” and give examples with “such as”.
I can compare good values and harmful habits in a short paragraph.

pages.title: A Lasting Legacy
pages.content:
Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“Whoever possesses patience rises to the heavens,
For within patience lies every kind of skill”
Turkish:
Sabır kimdeyise ol arşa süner
Ki sabr içinde bulınur dürlü hüner
[/POEM]

In another verse warning against anger and arrogance, he says:

[POEM]
English:
“Whoever is filled with anger loses their faith
If faith is required, one must give up anger and arrogance”
Turkish:
Buşu kimdeyise imanı gider
İman gerek ise vârını gider
[/POEM]

It is obvious that Yunus Emre was not only a prominent figure in his own time but also left a lasting legacy. His writings are valuable not only as literary works but also as a moral guide for future generations.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
a lasting influence or contribution passed on to later generations
important, widely recognized, or influential
the attitude of someone who feels superior to others and shows too much pride
has or holds a quality
people who will live after the present generation and inherit its cultural influence

hotspots.title: Patience and Anger
hotspots.description: Yunus’s verses praised patience, which holds every kind of skill, and warned that anger costs a person their faith.

hotspots.title: Guide for Generations
hotspots.description: Yunus Emre’s writings are valuable both as literary works and as a moral guide for future generations.

exercises.title: A Confident Conclusion
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use Chapter 13.
exercises.question: In the last paragraph, how does the writer present the claim that Yunus Emre left a lasting legacy?
options: as the writer’s own confident judgement
as a view that some historical sources report
as a claim Yunus makes about himself in a verse
as an uncertain idea that needs more evidence
exercises.explanation: The paragraph begins “It is obvious that …”: the writer speaks in their own voice and with strong certainty. The next sentence gives the reason: his writings are valuable “not only as literary works but also as a moral guide for future generations.”

feedback.correct: Yes. “It is obvious that” shows the writer’s own strong stance, not a reported or hedged claim.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first words of the last paragraph. Do they report someone else’s view, or do they show the writer’s own certainty?

languageFocusExercises.title: Verses on Patience and Anger
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line of Yunus Emre’s verses in Chapter 13 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do the verses teach about patience, anger and arrogance?

matchingPairs.left: “Whoever possesses patience rises to the heavens,”
matchingPairs.right: A person who can endure calmly reaches the highest spiritual rank.

matchingPairs.left: “For within patience lies every kind of skill”
matchingPairs.right: Every kind of ability is hidden inside calm endurance.

matchingPairs.left: “Whoever is filled with anger loses their faith”
matchingPairs.right: Uncontrolled rage takes away a person’s belief.

matchingPairs.left: “If faith is required, one must give up anger and arrogance”
matchingPairs.right: To keep your belief, you have to leave rage and pride behind.

correctAnswer.“Whoever possesses patience rises to the: A person who can endure calmly reaches the highest spiritual rank.
correctAnswer.“For within patience lies every kind of: Every kind of ability is hidden inside calm endurance.
correctAnswer.“Whoever is filled with anger loses thei: Uncontrolled rage takes away a person’s belief.
correctAnswer.“If faith is required, one must give up: To keep your belief, you have to leave rage and pride behind.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Whoever …” means “any person who …” and introduces a general truth. In “For within patience lies every kind of skill”, “For” means “because”, and the order is inverted for emphasis (every kind of skill lies within patience). The second verse moves from a result (losing faith) to a necessary action (“one must give up …”).

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each line with its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Read the two verses at the start of Chapter 13 again. Which lines speak about a reward, which about a hidden ability, which about a loss and which about what a person has to do?

languageFocusExercises.title: His Lasting Legacy
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines about his legacy?

transformItems.source: It is obvious that Yunus Emre was not only a prominent figure in his own time but also left a lasting legacy.
transformItems.frame: [blank], Yunus Emre was not only a prominent figure in his own time but also left a lasting legacy.

transformItems.source: It is obvious that Yunus Emre was not only a prominent figure in his own time but also left a lasting legacy.
transformItems.frame: It is obvious that Yunus Emre left a lasting legacy [blank] being a prominent figure in his own time.

transformItems.source: His writings are valuable not only as literary works but also as a moral guide for future generations.
transformItems.frame: His writings are valuable [blank] as literary works and as a moral guide for future generations.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It is obvious that …” and a stance adverb such as “Obviously” or “Clearly” both show that the writer is certain. “Not only … but also” can be rephrased with “in addition to / as well as + -ing”, or with “both … and” when the two parts are equal.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the writer’s certainty and both parts of the legacy.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Which one-word adverb means “it is obvious that”, and which structures add a second quality?

languageFocusExercises.title: Final Synthesis
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a 6–8 sentence conclusion about why Yunus Emre still matters.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why does Yunus Emre still matter?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The task asks learners to synthesize the whole book through B2 discourse rather than recall one fact.

feedback.correct: Well done. Check that each target pattern carries a clear relationship in your paragraph.
feedback.incorrect: Return to the chapter sentences that use these patterns and model your own sentences on them.

discussionPrompts.question: Cover language, history, Sufi thought and morals. Use “both … and” and “has continued to”.
discussionPrompts.example: Yunus Emre remains significant in this book for several connected reasons. He was one of the first to create poetry from the heart in plain Turkish, and his words helped Turkish to grow as a literary language. He lived in a time of uprisings, Mongol invasion and great suffering in Anatolia. In those hard days, he used poetry to help people make sense of life through his Sufi identity. His thought is built on tawhid, love and a pure heart. His verses also praise patience and warn against greed, anger and arrogance. For these reasons, his writings are valued both as literary works and as a moral guide. His legacy has continued to guide readers long after his own time.

beforeYouRead.question: Skim it: What is this chapter mainly about?
options: Yunus’s travels in Syria and Azerbaijan
Yunus’s verses on patience and anger, and his lasting legacy

iCan: I can explain why Yunus Emre’s legacy still matters.
I can add a second point with “not only … but also …” and “both … and …”.
I can write a conclusion that brings the whole book together.

groupTask.title: A Legacy in Evidence

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You copy two lines from your chapters exactly as they are written in the book.

roles.name: Explainer
roles.job: You explain what each line means and how strongly it supports the claim that Yunus Emre left a lasting legacy.

roles.name: Writer
roles.job: You write the text using at least three patterns from the Language Focus pages and add one realistic example from school life.

roles.name: Designer and Presenter
roles.job: You lay out the one-page poster or record the two-minute audio report and present it.

steps: Choose one strand of Yunus Emre’s legacy as the book presents it: Plain literary Turkish (Chapters 1–2), Sufi thought (Chapters 7–10) or moral guidance (Chapters 11–13).
Copy two lines exactly, for example: “His writings are valuable not only as literary works but also as a moral guide for future generations.” or “Love brings unity and harmony.”
Explain each line, then judge how strongly the book supports the legacy claim. Use patterns such as “According to …”, “not only … but also …” and “Whoever …”.
Add one realistic example from school life. Nobody speaks as Yunus Emre, Taptuk Emre or any other person from the book; you only report and explain what the book says.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its poster or plays its audio report, reads one exact quote aloud and says how strongly it supports the legacy claim.
groupTask.solo: Choose one strand, copy two exact lines, and write a short paragraph that explains them, judges how strong the evidence is and gives one example from school life.

legend.seljuk-pressure: Anatolian Seljuk lands under Mongol pressure

age.born: Yunus Emre is born around this time.
age.died: Yunus Emre dies around this time. He is about {years} old.

places.name: Anatolia
places.text: Yunus Emre was a great Anatolian poet and Sufi. According to the widely accepted view, he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21. In 1240, the Turkmen rebelled under the leadership of Baba Ishak. Throughout Yunus’s life, the Mongol storm swept across Anatolia, and he traveled around it as a wise dervish.
places.teacherNote: The book names no birthplace, lodge or grave, so the map shows only the region. Chapter 3: the Anatolian Seljuk Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I (1220–1237) established a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas; point to both sea names. The line from the east shows the Oguz and Turkmen tribes who migrated to Anatolia from Central Asia to escape the Mongol invasion (Chapter 4); its path is approximate.
places.question: How did Yunus Emre respond to people’s search for meaning in such hard days?

places.name: Konya
places.text: The Anatolian Seljuk state was also called the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya. As it grew weaker, small principalities quickly appeared in Anatolia. They were in constant conflict over the throne, wealth, and summer and winter pastures. At that time, the Ottoman state was still a small principality.
places.teacherNote: The B2 text names Konya only in the state’s name, “the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya” (Chapter 6). It does not call Konya the capital, so the card does not either.
places.question: What happened in Anatolia when the Anatolian Seljuk state grew weaker?

places.name: Erzurum, 1242
places.text: The Babai uprisings gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack. In late 1242, they captured Erzurum and killed its people with swords. This disaster caused deep sorrow and fear among the Anatolian Seljuks.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 5. The book does not describe the Mongols’ road; the army line from Azerbaijan to Erzurum is approximate.
places.question: Why did the Mongols in Azerbaijan feel ready to attack at this moment?

places.name: Kösedağ, 1243
places.text: In 1243, the Anatolian Seljuk army and the Mongols clashed at Kösedağ, 80 km northeast of Sivas. Using their classic false retreat and circling tactic, the Mongols wiped out the Anatolian Seljuk forces. After this easy victory, they destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri and Erzincan, leaving not a single stone standing. Women and children were taken captive and forced to follow the Mongol army.
places.teacherNote: The book gives the place as 80 km northeast of Sivas; the exact battlefield is not known, so the pin is approximate. Chapter 3 says the defeat at Kösedağ made the Mongols’ invasion of Anatolia easier.
places.question: The book says the Mongol storm swept across Anatolia “like a roller”. What does this image tell us?

places.name: Azerbaijan
places.text: In Yunus Emre’s time, there were Mongols in Azerbaijan. The Anatolian Seljuk forces stopped the Babai uprisings only with great difficulty, and this gave these Mongols the courage to attack. Their army then took Erzurum and fought at Kösedağ.
places.teacherNote: Medieval Azerbaijan was the land around Tabriz, mostly in north-west Iran today. It is not the same as the modern Republic of Azerbaijan. The pin is approximate.
places.question: How did the Babai uprisings open the way for the Mongol attack?

places.name: Iran
places.text: The Ilkhanate Empire was the Mongol state centred in Iran. In time, the Anatolian Seljuks became dependent on the Mongols, and a large part of the state’s income was sent to them every year. Finally, in 1308, the lands of Anatolia were directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire. Under Mongol pressure, shaykhs from Turkestan, Transoxiana, Khorasan, Khwarezm and Iran came to Anatolia.
places.teacherNote: The pin marks Iran as a region, not a city. Turkestan, Transoxiana, Khorasan and Khwarezm are farther east, off this map.
places.question: Why did the yearly tax make both the state and the people poorer?

challenge.prompt: Find Konya. The Anatolian Seljuk state was also called the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya.
Find Kösedağ, where the Anatolian Seljuk army and the Mongols clashed in 1243. It is 80 km northeast of Sivas.
Find Erzurum. The Mongols captured it in late 1242.
Find Erzincan. The Mongols plundered it after their victory at Kösedağ.
Find Azerbaijan. The Mongols who attacked the Anatolian Seljuks were there.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check whole-book comprehension with eight evidence-based questions.

exercises.title: More Than a School
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapters 2 and 3.
exercises.question: The story presents tekkes only as places of Sufi training, with no wider role in society or the arts.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “they were also important civil society organizations that strengthened social solidarity and cooperation” Chapter 3: “tekkes were leading institutions in the field of the fine arts, particularly poetry.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. The writer gives tekkes a social role in Chapter 2 and an artistic role in Chapter 3, where poets like Yunus were trained.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the last paragraph of Chapter 2 and the first paragraph of Chapter 3. What else were tekkes besides places of Sufi training?

exercises.title: From Glory to Decline
exercises.instructions: Connect Chapter 3 with Chapter 4 and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 3 calls the rule of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I the most glorious Seljuk period. What does Chapter 4 present as the start of the decline that followed?
options: the Babai rebellion led by the followers of Baba Ilyas
the Mongol capture of Erzurum at the end of 1242
the poor governance of his son, Kaykhusraw II
the constant conflict of the small principalities
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “The rule of the Anatolian Seljuk Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I (1220–1237) was the most powerful and glorious period of the Seljuks.” Chapter 4: “However, due to the poor governance of his son, Kaykhusraw II (1237–1246), the Seljuk economic and social structure began to decline.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. The word “However” marks the turn: the decline begins with the son’s weak rule, and his failure later “even worsened the social and economic chaos.”
feedback.incorrect: Look at the second sentence of Chapter 4, which begins with “However”. The other events in the options come later in the story.

exercises.title: Like a Roller
exercises.instructions: Choose the best reading of the writer’s image in Chapter 5.
exercises.question: The writer says the Mongol storm “swept across Anatolia like a roller”. What does this image suggest?
options: The Mongols won by pretending to retreat and then circling.
The attacks were sudden, but they did little lasting damage.
The destruction was wide and crushed everything in its path.
The Mongols moved through Anatolia without meeting any army.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Throughout Yunus’s life, this Mongol storm swept across Anatolia like a roller, leaving behind blood, misery, and ruins.”

feedback.correct: Yes. A roller flattens whatever lies in front of it, and the writer adds that it left “blood, misery, and ruins” behind.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the sentence with the image near the end of Chapter 5, and notice what the storm left behind. One option describes a tactic, not the image.

exercises.title: Sultans in Name
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 6.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 6, the agreement with the Mongols allowed the Seljuk sultans to go on ruling as independent rulers.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “In the end, an agreement was reached with the Mongols, but in time the Seljuks became a dependent state of the Mongols. The Seljuk sultans began to act almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. By comparing the sultans to “civil officials”, the writer shows that they no longer ruled in their own right.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 6. What did the Seljuks become after the agreement, and what does the writer compare the sultans to?

exercises.title: The Outer Side of Islam
exercises.instructions: Connect Chapter 1 with a later verse and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 1 says Sufis live within the outer and inner norms of Islam. Which of Yunus’s lines speaks most directly about the outer side, the body’s acts of worship?
options: “He should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers”
“The heart is the throne of the Lord, and He looked at the heart.”
“For within patience lies every kind of skill”
“I’ve fallen into the prison of greed and cannot escape”
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “The outer part relates to the body’s acts of worship, whereas the inner side handles the morality and intentions of the heart.” Chapter 9: “He should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers”

feedback.correct: Well done. Prayer is an act of worship done with the body. The other lines are about the heart and morality, the inner side.
feedback.incorrect: Reread how Chapter 1 defines the outer and the inner side. Then ask which line is about an act of worship, and which lines are about the heart and character.

exercises.title: A Guest in This World
exercises.instructions: Connect Chapter 11 with Chapter 1 and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: In Chapter 11 Yunus calls a person “a guest in this world”. Which Sufi principle from Chapter 1 does this image support most directly?
options: giving generously without expecting any return
not attaching importance to wealth, status and fame
doing good to all individuals without prejudice
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “Whoever comes into this world must eventually leave it, A guest in this world, one day they must set out for their homeland” Chapter 1: “not attaching importance to worldly possessions such as wealth, status, and fame.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. A guest does not settle down or hold on to what is in the house, so worldly wealth, status and fame lose their weight.
feedback.incorrect: Think about what a guest does and does not own. Then reread the list of Sufi principles at the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 1.

exercises.title: The Cost of Anger
exercises.instructions: Connect Chapter 9 with Chapter 13 and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 9 links anger to the absence of love. What further cost of anger does the verse in Chapter 13 add?
options: It can trap a person in a prison of greed.
It can cost a person their wealth and status.
It can bring heartbreak and separation.
It can cause a person to lose their faith.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “where love is absent, negative emotions such as anger, heartbreak and separation arise.” Chapter 13: “Whoever is filled with anger loses their faith”

feedback.correct: Yes. Chapter 9 shows anger growing where love is missing; Chapter 13 goes further and puts faith itself at risk.
feedback.incorrect: Heartbreak and separation are already in Chapter 9. Reread the verse after the words “warning against anger and arrogance” in Chapter 13.

exercises.title: More Than Endurance
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapters 12 and 13.
exercises.question: In Yunus’s verses on patience, patience is more than bearing hardship: It also leads to greatness and holds every kind of skill.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “Those blessed with patience will achieve greatness.” Chapter 13: “Whoever possesses patience rises to the heavens, For within patience lies every kind of skill”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The verses present patience as a source of greatness and skill, not only as a way to survive hard times.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the patience verses at the end of Chapter 12 and the start of Chapter 13. What do they say patience leads to?

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the story in one place.

vocabulary.definition: a spiritual tradition within Islam focused on inner purification and closeness to Allah
vocabulary.storyExample: A Sufi is a person who seeks closeness to Allah by adopting Islamic mysticism.

vocabulary.definition: extremely important to the development or outcome of something
vocabulary.storyExample: He was also one of the Turkish poets to play a crucial role in the development of Old Anatolian Turkish.

vocabulary.definition: standards that guide judgments about right conduct and character
vocabulary.storyExample: Sufis adhere to moral principles that include the pursuit of becoming better people, the ability to remain patient during difficult times, the act of giving generously without expecting any return, the act of doing good to all individuals without prejudice, the response to evil with kindness, and not attaching importance to worldly possessions such as wealth, status, and fame.

vocabulary.definition: in a willing and giving way, especially by giving more than is expected
vocabulary.storyExample: Sufis adhere to moral principles that include the pursuit of becoming better people, the ability to remain patient during difficult times, the act of giving generously without expecting any return, the act of doing good to all individuals without prejudice, the response to evil with kindness, and not attaching importance to worldly possessions such as wealth, status, and fame.

vocabulary.definition: a continuing body of writing shaped by shared styles, themes, or methods
vocabulary.storyExample: He established a literary tradition based on Sufism.

vocabulary.definition: a person who lived at the same time as another
vocabulary.storyExample: According to historical accounts, he was a contemporary of famous figures such as Haji Bektash Veli, Mevlana Jalal al-Din Rumi, and Saru Saltuk.

vocabulary.definition: unity and mutual support among members of a community
vocabulary.storyExample: At that time, tekkes were not just institutions that offered Sufi training but they were also important civil society organizations that strengthened social solidarity and cooperation and also received support from government officials of their time.

vocabulary.definition: organizations and groups that people form outside the government to serve the community
vocabulary.storyExample: At that time, tekkes were not just institutions that offered Sufi training but they were also important civil society organizations that strengthened social solidarity and cooperation and also received support from government officials of their time.

vocabulary.definition: Islamic educational institutions in which religious and other scholarly subjects are taught
vocabulary.storyExample: However, his education was not limited to madrasas.

vocabulary.definition: a person who guides another person in religious or spiritual development
vocabulary.storyExample: He also studied both divine love and morals at the tekke, which was a place where Sufi education was taught under the guidance of a sheikh (spiritual tutor).

vocabulary.definition: creative activities such as poetry, music and painting, valued for their beauty rather than their usefulness
vocabulary.storyExample: Besides, tekkes were leading institutions in the field of the fine arts, particularly poetry.

vocabulary.definition: happened during the same period as another event or condition
vocabulary.storyExample: The 13th and 14th centuries, the period in which Yunus Emre was born and lived, coincided with hard times.

vocabulary.definition: made something easier to happen or to achieve
vocabulary.storyExample: The defeat at Kösedağ facilitated the Mongols' invasion of Anatolia.

vocabulary.definition: the act of entering a territory by force, especially with an army
vocabulary.storyExample: The defeat at Kösedağ facilitated the Mongols' invasion of Anatolia.

vocabulary.definition: the branch of a state’s armed forces that operates at sea
vocabulary.storyExample: He expanded the country’s borders and established a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas.

vocabulary.definition: to become gradually weaker or less effective
vocabulary.storyExample: However, due to the poor governance of his son, Kaykhusraw II (1237–1246), the Seljuk economic and social structure began to decline.

vocabulary.definition: living by moving from place to place rather than settling permanently
vocabulary.storyExample: The nomadic Oguz and Turkmen tribes, who had migrated to Anatolia from Central Asia to escape the Mongol invasion, were exhausted from wandering and were looking for safe lands to settle in.

vocabulary.definition: weak or ineffective management of public affairs and political responsibilities
vocabulary.storyExample: However, due to the poor governance of his son, Kaykhusraw II (1237–1246), the Seljuk economic and social structure began to decline.

vocabulary.definition: a state of social tension, disturbance, or dissatisfaction
vocabulary.storyExample: This crowd of nomads was also causing unrest within the community.

vocabulary.definition: resisted or fought against established political authority
vocabulary.storyExample: In 1240, they rebelled under the leadership of Baba Ishak, who was a follower of Baba Ilyas.

vocabulary.definition: a military tactic in which a force pretends to withdraw in order to draw the enemy forward
vocabulary.storyExample: The Mongols, using the classic false retreat and circling tactic, wiped out the Seljuk forces.

vocabulary.definition: held as a prisoner by force, especially after a war
vocabulary.storyExample: They slaughtered the men with swords; women and children were taken captive and forced to follow the Mongol army.

vocabulary.definition: stopped or brought under control by force
vocabulary.storyExample: In the end, the Seljuk forces suppressed the rebellion with great difficulty and put the rebels to the sword.

vocabulary.definition: stole goods from a place by force, especially during war or disorder
vocabulary.storyExample: Following their easy victory at Kösedağ, the Mongols destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri, and Erzincan, leaving not a single stone standing.

vocabulary.definition: killed people in large numbers in a violent and brutal way
vocabulary.storyExample: They slaughtered the men with swords; women and children were taken captive and forced to follow the Mongol army.

vocabulary.definition: a state whose political freedom is limited by a stronger power
vocabulary.storyExample: In the end, an agreement was reached with the Mongols, but in time the Seljuks became a dependent state of the Mongols.

vocabulary.definition: assistance that reduces hardship, pressure, or suffering
vocabulary.storyExample: Statesmen like Jalal al-Din Karatay, while on the one hand trying to manage the Mongols, were also making efforts to provide some relief to the state and the people.

vocabulary.definition: small territories or states ruled by a prince, ruler, or local dynasty
vocabulary.storyExample: The weakening of the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya led to the rapid emergence of small principalities in Anatolia.

vocabulary.definition: a serious disagreement or struggle between groups or political powers
vocabulary.storyExample: They were also in constant conflict over the throne, wealth, and summer and winter pastures.

vocabulary.definition: joined or placed under the direct authority of another political entity
vocabulary.storyExample: Finally, in 1308, the lands of Anatolia were directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire (the Mongol state centred in Iran).

vocabulary.definition: a means or form through which ideas are communicated
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
vocabulary.storyExample: He tried to respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life in hard days through the lens of his Sufi identity, using poetry as his medium.

vocabulary.definition: loyal and sincere devotion to someone
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
vocabulary.storyExample: In his poems, he expresses a vivid love for Allah as a way of life, along with fear of Allah and faithfulness to the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

vocabulary.definition: a condition of extreme disorder in which normal structures no longer function effectively
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
vocabulary.storyExample: Anatolia was experiencing total chaos.

vocabulary.definition: members of Sufi traditions who follow a disciplined spiritual path
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
