pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the source-framing, cause-result, concession, comparison, interpretation, necessity and possibility patterns developed across all thirteen chapters.

exercises.title: Notice: Whose Claim Is It?
exercises.instructions: Whose claim is it? Put each sentence in the right group.
exercises.question: Is it from sources, from Yunus Emre, or from the writer?

dragDropGroups.group: The writer reports what sources or scholars say
items: Some sources note that he received a good madrasa education …
According to the widely accepted view, he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21.
Sources say: “The Mongols slaughtered the people of the great cities and towns …”

dragDropGroups.group: The writer reports Yunus Emre’s own view
items: For, according to him, where love is absent, negative emotions such as anger, heartbreak and separation arise.
In his view, purity of the heart is essential for the proper performance of acts of worship.
According to Yunus, morality consists of abandoning behaviors unbecoming of humans.

dragDropGroups.group: The writer makes the claim in their own voice
items: Society was struggling to cope with these trials.
These events created an atmosphere of panic in Anatolia that had never been seen before.
Anatolia was experiencing total chaos.

The writer reports what sources or schol: Some sources note that he received a good madrasa education …
According to the widely accepted view, he was born in 1240–41 and died in 1320–21.
Sources say: “The Mongols slaughtered the people of the great cities and towns …”
The writer reports Yunus Emre’s own view: For, according to him, where love is absent, negative emotions such as anger, heartbreak and separation arise.
In his view, purity of the heart is essential for the proper performance of acts of worship.
According to Yunus, morality consists of abandoning behaviors unbecoming of humans.
The writer makes the claim in their own: Society was struggling to cope with these trials.
These events created an atmosphere of panic in Anatolia that had never been seen before.

exercises.explanation: The book keeps three voices apart. “Some sources note”, “Sources say:” and “the widely accepted view” report historical sources or scholars, often where the details are uncertain. “According to him”, “In his view” and “According to Yunus” keep a religious or moral idea as Yunus’s own. Sentences with no frame are the writer’s own claims about the period. When you summarise the book, keep the frame: Do not turn a source’s report or Yunus’s view into a plain fact.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated the sources, Yunus’s view and the writer’s own voice.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the start of each sentence. Is there a frame such as “Some sources note” or “In his view”? If there is no frame, the writer is speaking.

exercises.title: Notice: Accept, Then Qualify
exercises.instructions: Read the three sentences. Then choose what the first word does.
exercises.question: Chapter 2: “However, his education was not limited to madrasas.” Chapter 6: “Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough.” Chapter 8: “Nonetheless, this multiple existence is nothing but manifestations of the names of Allah.” What do “However”, “Nevertheless” and “Nonetheless” do?
options: They show that the sentence before was wrong and should be forgotten.
They accept the sentence before and then add a point that limits it or goes against what we might expect from it.
They give the reason for the sentence before.
They introduce an example of the sentence before.
exercises.explanation: All three are linkers of concession. The earlier point stays true: Yunus had a good madrasa education; the statesmen did make efforts; unity did break into many things. The next sentence then limits it or goes against the expectation it creates. “Nevertheless” and “Nonetheless” are more formal than “However” and mean “even so”.

feedback.correct: Correct. A concession linker keeps the first point and qualifies it.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence before each one in its chapter. Is that earlier point cancelled, or is it still true?

exercises.title: Notice: Seen, Not Literally True
exercises.instructions: Read the two sentences. Is the statement true or false?
exercises.question: Chapter 5: “In the eyes of the Turkmen, these spiritual fathers were divine saviors.” Chapter 6: “The Seljuk sultans began to act almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials.” Statement: In both sentences, the writer states as a literal fact what these people really were.
exercises.explanation: False. “In the eyes of the Turkmen” limits the claim to how one group saw the fathers; the writer does not say that they really were saviors. “As if” + a past form (“were”) compares the sultans with officials and marks the comparison as not literally true, and “almost” softens it further. B2 writers use such frames to keep perception and interpretation apart from fact.

feedback.correct: Correct. One sentence reports a group’s perception; the other makes a non-literal comparison.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the frames: “In the eyes of …” and “almost as if …”. Whose view is it, and is the comparison literal?

exercises.title: Build: Contrast, Cause and Conclusion
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentences from the book with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which words show a contrast, a cause, a result and a conclusion?
exercises.fillBlanksText: The outer part relates to the body’s acts of worship, [blank] the inner side handles the morality and intentions of the heart. … Anatolia faced political, economic, and social hardships [blank] these assaults. … The weakening of the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya [blank] the rapid emergence of small principalities in Anatolia. … Love for the created is an extension of the love of Allah. [blank], those who love the Creator love the created, …
exercises.explanation: “Whereas” sets two sides of one lifestyle against each other. “As a result of” + a noun phrase gives the cause of the hardships; “because” would need a full clause with a verb, and “despite” would make the assaults something that did not stop the hardships, which is illogical. “Led to” + a noun phrase links a cause (the weakening) to its result (the emergence). “Therefore” opens a sentence that draws a conclusion from the one before.

feedback.correct: Well done. You chose each linker for its relationship and its grammar.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask two questions: Which relationship is it (contrast, cause, result, conclusion)? And what follows the gap: A clause, a noun phrase or a new sentence?

exercises.title: Build: No More Than the Book Says
exercises.instructions: Each sentence says too much. Tap the strong words, then choose a more careful version.
exercises.question: Can you make each sentence say only what the book says?

errorItems.sentence: If we take a closer look at this historical atmosphere, we can fully understand Anatolia …
All state income began to be sent to the Mongols every year.
He succeeded in responding to people’s efforts to make sense of life in hard days …

exercises.explanation: The writer measures each claim. Studying the historical atmosphere helps us understand Anatolia better, not completely. “A significant part of” state income went to the Mongols, not all of it. And Yunus “tried to respond”: “tried to” reports his effort without claiming success, while “succeeded in”, “managed to” and “was able to” claim that he achieved it.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the writer’s degree, quantity and certainty.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with the book: Chapter 3 (a closer look), Chapter 6 (state income) and Chapter 7 (Yunus’s response). Which word does the writer really use?

exercises.title: Build: Events as Nouns, Events as Verbs
exercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning as the book.
exercises.question: Can you change a verb into a noun, and a noun into a verb?

transformItems.source: He expanded the country’s borders and established a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas.
transformItems.frame: His rule saw the [blank] of the country’s borders and the establishment of a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas.

transformItems.source: Starting in the 13th century, the Turkmen population grew in Anatolia.
transformItems.frame: Starting in the 13th century, there was a [blank] in the Turkmen population in Anatolia.

transformItems.source: Following their easy victory at Kösedağ, the Mongols destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri, and Erzincan, …
transformItems.frame: After they had [blank] easily at Kösedağ, the Mongols destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri, and Erzincan.

exercises.explanation: History writing often packs an event into a noun: expand → expansion, grow → growth, win → victory. The noun can then be the subject or object of another verb, as in “The defeat at Kösedağ facilitated the Mongols’ invasion of Anatolia.” When a verb becomes a noun, an adverb becomes an adjective (they won easily → their easy victory). A clause with a verb shows more clearly who did what.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved between verbs and nouns without changing the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Find the event in each sentence from the book (expanded, grew, victory). Then give the noun or verb form that fits the new sentence.

exercises.title: Build: Two Sides in One Sentence
exercises.instructions: Choose the words that complete each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: Which words add a second idea to the first?

formChoices.sentence: At that time, tekkes were not just institutions that offered Sufi training [choice] they were also important civil society organizations …
He also studied [choice] divine love and morals at the tekke, …
Yunus Emre emphasizes not only the heart [choice] the intellect as a value, …

exercises.explanation: “Not just … but … also” and “not only … but also” keep the first side and add a second, often less expected one: Tekkes were training places and also civil society organizations; Yunus values the heart and also the intellect. “Both … and” joins two equal parts. “Either … or” would offer a choice and “neither … nor” would reject both, so they cannot go with “and”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each sentence keeps two sides together.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word that goes with the gap: “not just”, “and”, “not only”. Which word is its partner?

exercises.title: Use: The Old Covered Bazaar
exercises.instructions: This paragraph is not from the book. Complete it with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which words fit this report about an old bazaar?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Our class studied the history of the old covered bazaar in the center of our town. [blank] the town archive, it was built more than two hundred years ago. Some older residents say that it was once the busiest market in the region. In the 1990s, many of its shops closed [blank] the opening of large shopping centers. [blank], a group of craftspeople did not give up and kept their workshops open. Today the bazaar is not only a place for shopping [blank] a meeting point for families and visitors. It seems that caring for old places can protect them, although it cannot solve every problem.
exercises.explanation: “According to” names the source of a fact, and “Some older residents say that …” reports a memory without making it a certainty. “As a result of” + a noun phrase gives the cause (“because” would need a clause). “Nevertheless” accepts the closures and adds the craftspeople’s different choice. “Not only … but also” adds a second role. The last sentence qualifies the conclusion with “It seems that …” and “although …”, like the careful claims in the book.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new report.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Is it a source, a cause, a concession or a second role? Then check what follows: A noun phrase, a comma, or the second part of a pair.

exercises.title: Use: Careful Claims at School
exercises.instructions: These school sentences say too much. Write the missing words to make them careful.
exercises.question: In a class survey, 21 of 28 students chose a spring trip. What can we really say?

transformItems.source: Everyone in our class agrees that the school trip should be in spring.
transformItems.frame: [blank] students in our class think that the school trip should be in spring.

transformItems.source: The new sports hall caused all the problems in our school budget.
transformItems.frame: The new sports hall [blank] to the problems in our school budget.

transformItems.source: Our survey proves that students read less because of their phones.
transformItems.frame: Our survey [blank] that students read less because of their phones.

exercises.explanation: Careful writers match the claim to the evidence. A quantifier (“Most students”) replaces “Everyone” when not all agree. “Contributed to” names one cause among others instead of “caused all”. A reporting verb such as “suggests” or “indicates” shows that evidence supports a claim without proving it. The book does the same with “Some sources note”, “A significant part of” and “tried to”.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your claims now match the evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each sentence: How many people, how much of the cause, and how sure can we be? Choose a word that says only that much.

exercises.title: Use: Take a Position
exercises.instructions: Write 6–8 sentences: Should every class do a community project each term? Give your view carefully.
exercises.question: Should every class do a community project each term?
exercises.explanation: Example: “In my view, a community project each term would be not only useful for our town but also good for us as learners. According to our class survey, most students would like to take part. Some teachers note that students who help others often feel more responsible. Last year, our book collection led to a new reading corner in a village school. As a result of this project, many of us understood our neighbors better. Nevertheless, a project every term could take time away from exams. Therefore, I suggest short projects that are planned together with teachers. Our experience suggests that community work can support learning, although it cannot replace lessons.”

feedback.correct: Check your paragraph: A clear position; not only … but also; a source (According to …, Some … note that …); cause and result (as a result of, led to, Therefore); a concession (Nevertheless, However); a careful claim (most, suggests, may) instead of an overclaim.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give your view with two sides: “In my view, … would be not only … but also …”
discussionPrompts.example: In my view, a community project each term would be not only good for our neighbourhood but also useful for our own learning.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 2–3 — Give evidence and its source: “According to …, …” / “Some … note that …”
discussionPrompts.example: According to our town council’s website, the park near our school needs volunteers every spring. Some students note that they feel more confident after working in a team.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 4–5 — Give a cause and a result: “… led to …” / “As a result of …, …” / “Therefore, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Last term, our book collection led to a small library in the waiting room of the local hospital. Therefore, I believe that even short projects can make a real difference.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 6–8 — Make your claim careful: “Nevertheless, …” / “This suggests that …, although …”
discussionPrompts.example: Nevertheless, a project every term might be difficult before exams. This suggests that teachers and students should plan the timing together, although some classes may need fewer projects. A careful plan would keep the benefits without adding too much stress.

pages.content: Demonstrate whole-book mastery through the Final Challenge.

exercises.title: What “Thus” Connects
exercises.instructions: Read the start of Chapter 2 and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 2 says: “Thus, his works both have literary value and are easy to understand.” What does the word “Thus” connect?
options: the simplicity of his style and his madrasa education
his famous contemporaries and the birth of Sufi literature
his knowledge of Arabic and his poems written in Persian
his balanced style and works that are both valuable and clear
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2 begins: “His style is neither too simple nor too complex. Thus, his works both have literary value and are easy to understand.” The balance in the first sentence is the cause; the value and clarity in the second are the result.

feedback.correct: Exactly. Because the style is neither too simple nor too complex, the works can be both literary and easy to read.
feedback.incorrect: “Thus” links a cause to a result. Look at the sentence just before it: What is said about his style?

exercises.title: A Restless Crowd
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer the text supports.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 4, why were the nomadic Oguz and Turkmen tribes causing unrest?
options: They had fled the Mongols and had no safe land to settle in.
They wanted to replace the sultan with a Mongol governor.
They refused to pay the yearly tax sent to the Mongols.
They were fighting the small principalities for pastures.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “The nomadic Oguz and Turkmen tribes, who had migrated to Anatolia from Central Asia to escape the Mongol invasion, were exhausted from wandering and were looking for safe lands to settle in. This crowd of nomads was also causing unrest within the community.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Tired from wandering and without safe land, the newcomers added to the unrest that Kaykhusraw II failed to manage.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the sentence about the nomadic tribes in the first paragraph of Chapter 4. The tax and the principalities belong to Chapter 6.

exercises.title: Three Kinds of Intellect
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer the text supports.
exercises.question: In Chapter 10, which type of intellect guides a person to behave with piety?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10: “According to him, there are three types of intellect: the practical reason, which enables a person to understand how the world works and sustain worldly life; the limited intellect, which teaches a person about the order of the hereafter; and the universal intellect, which guides one to behave with piety.”

feedback.correct: Right. The practical reason serves worldly life, the limited intellect teaches about the hereafter, and the universal intellect guides to piety.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the last sentence of Chapter 10 and match each type of intellect with what it does.

exercises.title: A Small Principality
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 6.
exercises.question: When the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya grew weak, the Ottoman state was already a large power in Anatolia.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “The weakening of the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya led to the rapid emergence of small principalities in Anatolia. They were also in constant conflict over the throne, wealth, and summer and winter pastures. The Ottoman state was still a small principality at that time.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. The Ottomans were only one of the small principalities that appeared as the Seljuks weakened.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 6. What does the writer say about the Ottoman state at that time?

exercises.title: Shaykhs and Dervishes
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 7.
exercises.question: The shaykhs who came to Anatolia under Mongol pressure trained dervishes, and these dervishes had strong influence among the nomads.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “During the same period, the shaykhs from the regions of Turkestan, Transoxiana, Khorasan, Khwarezm and Iran came to Anatolia under Mongol pressure. These shaykhs raised dervishes on their teachings; these dervishes were dominant among nomads.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. These dervishes spread a simple understanding of Islam and a kind of popular Sufism.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 7. Whom did the shaykhs raise, and among whom were they dominant?

exercises.title: Words in Context
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning in the text.
exercises.question: What does each word mean in its sentence?

matchingPairs.right: a person living at the same time
put an end to by force
robbed of goods by force
the coming into being

correctAnswer.contemporary: a person living at the same time
correctAnswer.suppressed: put an end to by force

exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “he was a contemporary of famous figures such as Haji Bektash Veli, Mevlana Jalal al-Din Rumi, and Saru Saltuk.” Chapter 5: “the Seljuk forces suppressed the rebellion with great difficulty” and “the Mongols destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri, and Erzincan”. Chapter 6: “The weakening of the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya led to the rapid emergence of small principalities in Anatolia.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Read each word in its sentence in Chapters 2, 5 and 6 and test the meanings there.

exercises.title: Who Is Who?
exercises.instructions: Match each name with what the text says about it.
exercises.question: What does the text say about each of these?

feedback.correct: Yes. You placed each name in its chapter.

exercises.title: Love for the Created

exercises.question: How does Yunus relate love for people to the love of Allah?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Love for the created is an [blank] of the love of Allah.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “He places love at the foundation of the human relationship with the Creator and with His creation. Love for the created is an extension of the love of Allah.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Loving the created is not separate from loving Allah; it grows out of it.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the third paragraph of Chapter 9. Love for the created continues from the love of Allah.

exercises.title: A Pure Heart
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 10 with one word: purity, strength, size or silence.
exercises.question: What does Yunus see as essential for worship to be done properly?
exercises.fillBlanksText: In his view, [blank] of the heart is essential for the proper performance of acts of worship.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10: “In his view, purity of the heart is essential for the proper performance of acts of worship. At the same time, the heart is the eye that perceives the truth and the center of understanding.”

feedback.correct: Yes. For Yunus, outer worship needs an inner condition: A pure heart.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the paragraph after the verse about the throne of the Lord in Chapter 10.

exercises.title: A Century of Storms
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order they happened.
exercises.question: In what order did these events take place?

sequencingItems.text: The Seljuks are defeated at Kösedağ.
The rule of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I comes to an end.
Anatolia is attached to the Ilkhanate Empire.
The Turkmen rebel under Baba Ishak.

exercises.explanation: Ala al-Din Kayqubad I ruled until 1237 (Chapter 3). The Turkmen rebelled in 1240 (Chapter 4). The Mongols took Erzurum in late 1242 and won at Kösedağ in 1243 (Chapter 5). Anatolia was attached to the Ilkhanate in 1308 (Chapter 6). Yunus died in 1320–21 (Chapter 2).

feedback.correct: Yes. Yunus lived his whole life in the century of crisis that followed the Seljuk golden age.
feedback.incorrect: Use the dates in Chapters 2 to 6. The rebellion came before the Mongol attacks.
